episode.throughLine: A young woman constrained at home secured a marriage arrangement, sought private teaching when university access failed, and completed mathematical research amid continuing difficulty.

contentProfile.contentNote: Family control, exclusion from university study, and exhaustion; no diagnosis or claim that achievement resolves suffering.

facts.statement: Sonia's sister and her friend proposed a marriage arrangement to a young student who wanted to study in Germany; he offered to marry Sonia.

sourceRefs.locator: pp. 17-18, from 'Aniuta and Inez' through 'Sonia for his wife'

sourceRefs.locator: pp. 19-24, especially p. 24 opening and age at foot

facts.statement: Sofia Kovalevskaya was a mathematician who developed a theory of partial differential equations, equations involving rates of change in several variables.

sourceRefs.locator: Title: Zur Theorie der partiellen Differentialgleichungen; author Sophie Kowalevsky
Biography, doctorate and professorship statements

arc.canonicalText: She was in the room she shared with her sister, before a family dinner. She was eighteen. In her account, their new dresses lay ready to be put on. Their mother was shopping, and their father was at his club. Elsewhere in the house, the governess and a maid were preparing the drawing-room. The sisters were alone. She could not simply go out by herself. She and her sister were required to have someone with them outside the house. For now, the family was busy getting ready to receive its guests. The dresses were waiting.
arc.sourceNote: Memory cue covers the remembered dinner scene, not an independently recorded transcript. No exact wedding month is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: Her father had refused to let her marry the young student. The refusal threatened her chance to leave home and continue studying. The arrangement had begun with her sister and a friend. They had approached a student who wanted to study abroad himself. He had agreed to the plan, but wanted the younger sister as his wife. Their father rejected that proposal. Now the family was preparing to return to its country home. The new interests she and her sister had found seemed about to be taken away. She wanted to continue her studies. The dinner clothes lay ready in their room.
arc.sourceNote: CRAFT HOLD: the refusal is recollected background within the dressing-room moment, not a sourced contemporaneous exchange. It is not permissible to invent the father's words or relocate his refusal into this room.

arc.canonicalText: She slipped out of the house alone while everyone was occupied. Her sister went down with her and kept watch at the gate. She walked quickly along the broad streets, which were nearly empty. It was getting dark. She had pulled her veil down close to her face. In the darkness of the stairs she was afraid. She climbed to the student's door and knocked. He opened it and led her into his study. Books stood in piles on the tables and chairs. There was a cleared space for her on a shaky sofa. She sat and waited.
arc.sourceNote: One continuous departure and arrival, reconstructed from pp. 20-21. CRAFT HOLD: the walking action crosses locations, rather than remaining strictly within one place.

arc.canonicalText: Her note asked her father to stop opposing the marriage. He came to the room where she was waiting. By the end of dinner, he introduced the student as her future husband. They married, and eventually she was able to study abroad. That did not end the restrictions. After studying in one university town, she moved to another to study with a particular professor. There the university did not admit women. She applied to the professor himself for private lessons. He distrusted this unfamiliar applicant. He gave her problems he had prepared for his advanced students. He expected her to be unable to solve them. She had the problems.
arc.sourceNote: Open compression from 1868 to autumn 1870; no assertion that marriage opened enrollment or that she never obtained permission. Problems were advanced; no invented motive that he deliberately sought to drive her away.

arc.canonicalText: In the professor's memory, she returned a week later with her solutions. She told him she had solved all the problems. He did not believe her. He asked her to sit beside him, then began examining what she had brought. He read the solutions one at a time. They were correct. They also showed ways of thinking that surprised him. She took off her hat in her eagerness. Her short curls were uncovered, and she blushed as he praised her work. He had expected her to fail the test he had set. Now he was reading the work beside its author. His praise reached her there.
arc.sourceNote: Memory from Weierstrass, reported by Leffler, pp. 34-35; confidence remains probable. Hat, curls and blush are source particulars. No invented dialogue, rereading, change of posture, or instant university admission.

arc.canonicalText: Private lessons followed, and the professor became a lasting friend. He visited her once a week. On Sunday evenings, she came to him. She worked with him for four years. At home she bent over her papers for long stretches, then returned to work after a hurried supper. Her companion described poor food and lodgings, and little rest. The work did not make daily life easy. At twenty-four, she received a doctorate on the strength of the research she had submitted. The award was made without requiring her to be present. She returned home exhausted and was unable to work for a time. She had finished the papers.
arc.sourceNote: Ends at the 1874 doctorate and immediate return, not Stockholm or the later prize. The companion's account supplies difficulty, not a diagnosis. Modern institutional account controls doctorate date; memoir wedding month is unresolved.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Sofia Kovalevskaya.

She was a mathematician who studied equations describing how several quantities change together. Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you. You are allowed to want room for something that matters to you. You do not have to feel ready.
arc.sourceNote: Reveal only. No instruction, outcome promise, achievement comparison or claim that hardship produced talent.

dramatizationLimits: Only source-attested action and feeling; no invented dialogue, chronology or motivation.
Leffler's reports of others' memories remain probable and use a brief prose memory cue.
Do not adopt Leffler's moral judgments, romantic psychologizing or speculative causes of death.
avoidRules: Keep names, years, institutions and named places out of passages before the bridge.
Do not imply a marriage instantly enabled university enrollment.
Do not turn academic work into a cure for exhaustion or family conflict.
Maintain the source and craft holds pending independent review.
